item.description:
DUBAI, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Washington's hostility towards Tehran will not change through partisan shifts or any concessions to the US, and those who believe otherwise are “greatly mistaken”, Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Wednesday, following the Republican Party's defeats in the US midterm elections.

item.title: Democratic Congress could test decades of US support for Israel
item.description:
By Patricia Zengerle

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats’ takeover of Congress and growing Republican unease over Israel could trigger the biggest reassessment of US support for its closest Middle East ally in decades, after an election shaped in part by anger over the Iran war.

Democrats won both the Senate and House in Tuesday’s midterms. Many winning candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

item.title: Morocco says it will uphold Western Sahara ceasefire after UN mission ends
item.description:
By Ahmed Eljechtimi

RABAT, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Morocco will stay committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara despite the end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the territory, the Royal Palace said on Wednesday.

The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission came to an end after the Security Council did not renew its mandate last week, the UN said on Sunday, removing the international presence that has monitored the ceasefire in the decades-old dispute.

item.title: Red Cross delivers essential medical supplies to Yemen's besieged Taiz city
item.description:
By Olivia Le Poidevin

GENEVA, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The Red Cross said on Wednesday it had delivered four truckloads of essential medical supplies to the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz after renewed fighting cut off access for weeks.

Taiz has been largely isolated for a month, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering the city and restricting the movement of civilians, after an escalation in clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement.

item.title: Turkey says EU comments on its rights record, judiciary are 'prejudiced, unfair'
item.description:
ANKARA, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Ankara rejected on Wednesday what it called the "prejudiced and unfair" stance of the European Union towards fundamental rights and the judiciary in Turkey, and regarding Cyprus, contained in the bloc's report on EU membership candidates.

In its annualenlargement policy report, the European Commission said that while the EU had advanced ties with Turkey in areas of mutual interest, legal action by Turkish authorities against elected officials, opposition figures and civil society hadraised concerns about Ankara's "adherence to core democratic principles".

item.title: Garment workers’ pay raised in Bangladesh after protests
item.description:
DHAKA: Bangladesh’s garment wage board agr­eed on Wednesday to raise minimum pay in the key export sector, but details remained scarce and it was unclear whether the deal would end five days of protests and clashes.

Tens of thousands of workers marched through industrial areas on Wedne­sday morning demanding hi­­­­g­­her wages, with some thr­­owing bricks, torching police vehicles and erecting barricades, as police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.

Protests eased in the afternoon after an agreement was announced, but there was no immediate indication that workers would return to factories and restart production. Many workers were still unsure what the announcement meant, union leader Kamrul Hasan of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation said, adding that most “did not know” how the wage board worked and were asking on social media whether their pay had increased.

Mahmudul Hasan, Ban­gl­adesh Garment Manuf­acturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) president, said workers should go back to work. “The unrest should subside, as progress is evident now,” Hasan said.

The Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee announced this in a notice. It said the examination schedule would be published later on the respective education boards' websites.

HSC results 2026 re-scrutiny applications open from Sunday

Currently, under the existing system for public examinations such as the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and HSC, candidates who fail in one or more subjects have to wait a year to retake the examinations.

They can choose to sit for only the subjects they failed or retake all subjects.

As a result, students who fail in just one or two subjects have to wait an entire year for another opportunity.

HSC results re-scrutiny: Applications open, here’s how to apply

The HSC and equivalent examinations concluded on 31 October.

Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee Liu Haixing arrived in Dhaka on Tuesday night on a three-day visit to Bangladesh.
During his visit, Liu is scheduled to meet President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. He will also attend a political dialogue, programs on Bangladesh-China relations and other engagements.
He arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 11pm on Tuesday aboard an Emirates Airlines flight, said Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony.
BNP Standing Committee Member and Prime Minister's Public Administration Affairs Adviser Ismail Zabiullah, BNP Vice Chairman Air Vice Marshal (Retd) Altaf Hossain Chowdhury and BNP Joint Secretaries General Khairul Kabir Khokon, Syed Emran Saleh Prince, Advocate Abdus Salam Azad and Prime Minister's Protocol Officer Kamrul Islam, among others, welcomed the Chinese delegation at the airport.
Liu will begin his engagements on Wednesday at 8:20am by paying homage at the mausoleums of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in the capital.
He is scheduled to pay a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Bangladesh Secretariat at 10:00 am on the same day.
The Chinese delegation accompanying Liu during the meeting will include Chinese Embassy Charge d'Affaires in Dhaka Dr Liu Yuyin, Director General of the CPC International Department's Bureau of Southeast and South Asian Affairs Peng Xiubin, Director General of its Public
Information and Communication Bureau Hu Zhaoming, Deputy Director General-level official of the Bureau of Southeast and South Asian Affairs Li Jinyan, Director of the same bureau Wang Siqi, and Deputy Division Director of the department's General Office and Minister's Assistant Liu Chengxiao.
The delegation also includes English interpreter Shi Meiqi and department officials Chen Yongpei, Zhang Guyu, Liu Hongru and He Yiyang.
Following the meeting with the Prime Minister, Liu will pay a courtesy call on the President at Bangabhaban at 11am. He will also visit Bangabhaban and attend a welcome luncheon hosted by the President.

He is also scheduled to attend the inauguration of the Bangladesh-China Centre for Party and State Governance Studies at the event.
Liu will visit the Bangladesh National Museum from 3:45pm before visiting the site of the former Chinese Embassy chancery building and the current chancery in Dhaka.
In the evening, he will attend a dinner hosted by Prime Minister's Political Adviser and BNP Acting Secretary General Advocate Ruhul Kabir Rizvi at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel at 7pm.
On the final day of his visit on Thursday, Liu will attend a livelihood support distribution programme at Shamsul Haque Khan School and College at 8:45am.
He will then join a breakfast meeting with Foreign Affairs State Minister Humaiun Kobir at the State Guest House Padma.

item.title: Journalists’ views to get priority in finalizing Cyber Security Act draft
item.description:
A meeting at the Posts and Telecommunications Division in Dhaka on Wednesday emphasized giving priority to the views of journalists and media representatives in finalizing the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026.
The meeting also placed particular weight on ensuring that the law is not used in any way as a tool to harass journalists, the media or independent journalism.
The meeting of the cabinet committee formed to review and finalize the draft of the Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 was held on Wednesday at the meeting room of the Posts and Telecommunications Division with Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam in the chair, according to a ministry press release.
The meeting held detailed discussions on the opinions of various stakeholders, recommendations of journalists and observations of the ministries and agencies concerned.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam were present.
For the protection of journalists and the media, the meeting discussed and reached an in-principle consensus on keeping a provision requiring prior permission from the court having jurisdiction before arresting any journalist, media owner or responsible person over news published or broadcast in the media, said the release.
It added that emphasis was also laid on following due legal process and preventing harassment in taking action against journalists.
The meeting also discussed a proposal to consider defamation, disparagement and cyberbullying separately and to rearrange the relevant sections of the law. It also discussed making the definition of cyberspace more specific.
Importance was also given to maintaining consistency with the Penal Code in the definition of and punishment for defamation. Opinions were also given on making the definitions of rumor and disinformation clearer and more specific so that press freedom is not undermined by vague or overly broad definitions in the law.
The meeting also discussed not including a provision for mobile courts in the law, informing the person or organization concerned of the reasons when content is removed or blocked, and fixing a timeframe for disposing of applications to unblock blocked content.
A proposal to issue a written notice and give an opportunity for self-defense before taking action against any media outlet or organization was also discussed.
The meeting also discussed the composition of the Cyber Security Council, media representation and consultation with international stakeholders.
Emphasis was laid on the concerned ministry holding discussions in coordination with development partners, including the United Nations, and international technology platforms such as Meta.
The meeting discussed refining the amended draft law further on the basis of stakeholders' opinions and recommendations and publishing it on the website. Emphasis was laid on making the draft more acceptable, effective and timely by taking public opinion.
Speakers at the meeting said the Cyber Security law must be framed by maintaining a balance between preventing cybercrime and protecting citizens' rights, freedom of expression and press freedom.
They said efforts to finalize the draft, taking into account the constructive opinions of all stakeholders concerned, will continue.
A presentation was made at the meeting on behalf of the National Cyber Security Agency.
Senior officials of the ministries and divisions concerned were present at the meeting.

item.title: Government plans to procure 5,830 vehicles for police
item.description:
A long-standing shortage of transport in the police force is set to be addressed through a major government initiative to procure 5,830 vehicles at a cost of Tk6,608 crore, aimed at improving mobility and strengthening field operations.
The proposed fleet includes pickup vans, jeeps, buses, ambulances, prison vans, speedboats, riot-control vehicles, armoured vehicles and specialised vehicles suitable for operations in remote and difficult-to-access areas.
The vehicles will be procured under two separate projects. Of the total allocation, Tk4,328 crore has been proposed for the purchase of 4,829 operational vehicles, while Tk2,280.14 crore will be spent on 1,001 specialized vehicles. The projects also include provisions for training police personnel in vehicle operation, repair and maintenance.
The main objective is to strengthen the police force's capacity to combat crime, conduct regular patrols, respond quickly to emergencies and maintain public order.
The two projects were placed for approval at the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) meeting on Wednesday. Following approval, the projects are scheduled to be implemented between October 2026 and June 2029.
According to the home ministry, police provide services across nearly 147,000 square kilometres of the country through 639 administrative police stations. However, the force currently has only 1,237 vehicles to serve these areas, meaning that each police station has fewer than two vehicles on average. Around 64% of the existing vehicles are more than 10 years old.
In addition, 455 police vehicles were burnt across the country during the 2024 student-people uprising, while another 1,074 vehicles were damaged. This further aggravated the shortage.
The ageing vehicles frequently break down during operations, making regular patrols, crime prevention and rapid responses to emergencies increasingly difficult.
Home ministry officials said many police stations have to manage law and order across their entire jurisdictions with just one pickup van. Ensuring an adequate supply of vehicles has therefore become essential. The addition of new vehicles is expected to improve police mobility at the field level and enable the rapid deployment of personnel and equipment when needed.
Asked about the initiative, Mirza Mohammad Ali Reza, joint secretary of the Planning-1 Wing of the Home Ministry of Home Affairs, said two projects had been sent to the Planning Commission to strengthen police capacity.
"A total of 5,830 vehicles will be procured to enhance the operational capacity of the police," he said.
"Many police stations have only one pickup van. How can they maintain law and order with that? How can the police perform their duties without the necessary logistical support?" he added.
Under the project titled “Procurement of Operational Vehicles for Capacity Enhancement of Bangladesh Police,” the government has proposed purchasing 4,829 vehicles at an estimated cost of Tk4,328 crore.
Double-cabin pickup vans account for the largest share of the proposed procurement. A total of 2,909 pickups will be purchased at an estimated cost of Tk2,501.74 crore, with each vehicle priced at Tk86 lakh.
The project also includes 400 jeeps with 2,700cc engines for senior police officials at a cost of Tk676 crore. Another 345 jeeps with 2,000cc engines will be procured at an estimated cost of Tk258.75 crore.
In addition, the government plans to purchase 214 microbuses at Tk52 lakh each, 148 non-air-conditioned large buses at the same unit price and 148 air-conditioned minibuses at Tk1.20 crore each. These vehicles will be used for the transportation of police personnel and to support the activities of different units.
The list of operational vehicles also includes 115 prison vans, 100 patrol cars and 50 ambulances.
To strengthen police operations along river routes, the project proposes procuring 100 speedboats at a cost of Tk80 crore.
The second project aims to strengthen the police force's capacity to handle special situations, maintain public order, investigate crimes and conduct operations in remote areas, alongside its regular activities.
Under the project titled “Procurement of Specialised Vehicles for Capacity Enhancement of Bangladesh Police,” 1,001 specialised vehicles will be purchased at an estimated cost of Tk2,280.14 crore.
To deal with situations such as labour unrest in industrial areas, the project proposes purchasing 11 armoured personnel carriers (APCs) at a cost of Tk132 crore.
For maintaining public order and managing potentially volatile gatherings, 20 water cannons, each with a capacity of 10,000 litres, will be procured at a cost of Tk128 crore.
The proposal also includes 20 crowd-control vehicles at a cost of Tk220 crore and 15 SWAT vans at Tk187 crore for specialised police units and bomb disposal teams.
Another 100 specialised patrol cars will be purchased at a cost of Tk56 crore to facilitate rapid operations during emergencies.
For the safe transportation of arrested individuals, the project proposes procuring 13 specialised vans at a cost of Tk43 crore. In addition, 55 prison vans will be purchased at Tk33 crore to transport detainees between police stations, courts and prisons.
To strengthen patrols and operations in remote and difficult-to-access areas, the project includes 50 all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and 100 hill motorcycles for use in hilly regions.
Another 200 high-speed motorcycles will be procured at an estimated cost of Tk160 crore.
The project also includes 50 utility terrain vehicles at a cost of Tk55 crore to transport police-trained dogs.
For intelligence operations and field-level information gathering, six mobile surveillance vehicles will be purchased at a cost of Tk114 crore.
To strengthen police operations in riverine and coastal areas, 15 quick-response boats or speedboats will be procured at a cost of Tk150 crore. Another 15 rescue boats will be purchased to help rescue people stranded in water or involved in accidents.
The proposed specialised fleet also includes 105 commander's suburban vehicles for the transportation of field-level unit commanders, 80 freezer vans for transporting bodies and 80 small deployment utility vehicles for police personnel deployed during elections, religious festivals and public gatherings.
In addition, 10 specialised vehicles will be procured to transport horses used in police ceremonial activities and training.
The two projects do not focus solely on purchasing vehicles. They also place emphasis on ensuring their proper operation, repair and maintenance through specialised training for police personnel.
Under the operational vehicles project, 650 personnel will receive training in light vehicle driving and mechanics, while 300 will be trained in heavy vehicle driving and mechanics. Another 50 personnel will receive training in vehicle repair.
Under the specialised vehicles project, 910 personnel will receive training in driving and mechanics, while another 50 will receive specialised mechanical training.
The operational vehicles project also proposes allocating Tk1.5 crore for purchasing equipment and machinery required for vehicle maintenance and repair.
Home Secretary Manzur Morshed Chowdhury told reporters that some specialised vehicles were also being procured for police personnel who would participate in United Nations peacekeeping missions.
He said the United Nations would reimburse the expenditure incurred for those vehicles at a later stage.
Officials concerned said rapid communication, necessary equipment and appropriate vehicles for different situations were essential to modern policing.
With specialised vehicles, police will be better equipped to overcome the limitations of conventional patrol cars and respond more quickly to emergencies in remote areas and along river routes.
The use of mobile command centres to coordinate the activities of different field units, along with specialised vehicles for crime-scene inspections, is also expected to make investigations more efficient.
The addition of rescue boats will further strengthen the police force's ability to assist people during floods, waterway accidents and other emergencies.
Officials expect the initiative to significantly reduce the police force's vehicle shortage once the projects are implemented. This, in turn, is expected to improve police services across the country, strengthen crime prevention, ensure faster responses to emergencies and enhance public safety.

item.title: RMG workers to get higher pay from January
item.description:
The newly reconstituted Minimum Wage Board for the ready-made garment (RMG) sector held its first meeting on Wednesday, announcing that the new wage structure will come into effect in December and workers will receive their increased wages from January 2027.
The timeline was announced jointly by the board’s owner representative ABM Shamsuddin and worker representative Babul Akhter after the meeting at the Minimum Wage Board office in Segunbagicha.
The meeting was chaired by newly appointed board Chairman and District and Sessions Judge Syed Azad Subhani.
The first meeting of the reconstituted board was held amid ongoing labour unrest in the garment sector and a series of high-level discussions over workers’ demands for higher wages.
Briefing reporters after the meeting, Syed Azad Subhani said the owner and worker representatives would submit their respective wage proposals at the next meeting.
The board’s neutral member will also submit a proposal following which formal discussions on the proposed wage rates will begin, he said.
The government reconstituted the Minimum Wage Board on Sunday through a gazette notification.
On Tuesday evening, BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to discuss the situation in the apparel sector.
After the meeting, Mahmud Hasan Khan told editors of major national dailies that an early announcement of the wage board’s timeline would help reassure garment workers and restore stability in the sector.

item.title: CVS is splitting into two companies: Healthcare giant’s ‘Pharmacy’ breakup explained
item.description:
CVS is breaking up.

On Wednesday, the healthcare giant announced plans to split into two separate, independent companies, and both will be publicly traded. 

The two companies will form a “leading healthcare solutions company” called CVS Health, and will encompass Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.

The second company, dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will be made up of roughly 9,000 CVS pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic, and the Health100 tech services business.

The company also announced that current CVS Health chair and CEO David Joyner will serve as CEO of the “new” CVS Health, and Prem Shah, current Group President of CVS Health, will be the CEO of the “new” CVS Pharmacy.

“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access, and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination.”

CVS shares were down approximately 12% on Wednesday morning.

As for the reason for the split?

Notably, the move effectively reverses, in some respects, the 2018 merger between CVS Health and Aetna.

According to company leadership, two smaller companies would be able to be more efficient and nimble than one single, larger one. When the dust settles, CVS Pharmacy will basically be a pharmacy company, while CVS Health will be focused on insurance and other services.

Regulatory concerns may also be at play. For example, The New York Times reports that some states, such as Arkansas and Tennessee, have passed laws in recent years that prevent large conglomerates from managing prescription benefits while simultaneously running retail and mail-order pharmacy services. 

Other companies have taken on similar strategies in recent years. Notably, Comcast is breaking off its media and technology businesses, it announced earlier this year, which likewise follows NBCUniversal’s decision to spin off some of its brands into another company, Versant.

Further, Madison Square Garden Sports is spinning off its pro sports franchises (the NHL’s New York Rangers and the NBA’s New York Knicks) into separate companies. And Keurig Dr Pepper recently announced plans to spin off its coffee division.

item.title: Google announces it will cut off internet search access for schools that reject AI
item.description:
Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence, the tech giant said Tuesday.

The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.

On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.

“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”

But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.

Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.

“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.

Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.

Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.

“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP Technology Writer

item.title: In Its Race to Field AI, The Pentagon’s Testing Can’t Keep Up
item.description:
CNN reported, citing four sources familiar with the episode, that the U.S. military prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel after an AI-assisted intelligence report misidentified its cargo. According to CNN, the report incorrectly concluded that the ship was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. Some of CNN’s sources said troops prepared to board the vessel and military aircraft were already airborne. Officials discovered the error before the planned operation. CNN could not establish which chatbot the analyst used and reported that the Pentagon and U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific did not respond to its requests for comment.

Military organizations use different tools and standards to check AI-generated information. As CNN reported, there is "no one set of standards for how the US verifies the information generated by these tools." The January 2026 AI Acceleration Strategy directs that the department enable “the latest models to be deployed within 30 days of public release". The model behind any application can change every month, but the definition of a correct answer should not. The fix, and the department's best path to AI safety, is to put guardrails in place by testing the systems built on these models the same way the department tests everything else it fields: against a written specification, by someone who does not work for the vendor, with evidence that outlasts any one model.

Scott Cohen is co-founder and CEO of Jaxon.AI, which sells AI verification and validation tools, including under Air Force and Space Force contracts. Jen Warren advises Jaxon.AI. The company could benefit financially if the Pentagon adopts the testing requirements recommended in this article.

A Model Is a Component

The department is dedicated to fielding AI quickly and widely. GenAI.mil launched in December 2025 with Google's Gemini; by September 2026 it had 1.7 million users. ChatGPT and Grok were added August 31, 2026. Users have built more than 100,000 custom agents since launch. On September 23, 2026, the deputy under secretary for research and engineering said the department will "proliferate frontier models" onto the secret and top secret networks next.

The directive on autonomy in weapon systems requires that "any further changes to the system will undergo appropriate V&V and T&E," that is, verification and validation, and test and evaluation. The department's own testers admit in a 2025 guidebook that "T&E of GenAI is still in its infancy as a discipline." The whole field shares the problem. Generative AI is particularly hard to test because a traditional test compares a system's output to a known right answer, and generative AI writes answers no one has seen before. There is no answer key to check them against.

The eight public announcements we reviewed, issued between December 2025 and September 23, 2026, did not disclose what performance tests GenAI.mil models underwent, what standards applied, or who signed off on fielding them. Every announcement cites Impact Level 5 accreditation instead, and the Chief Information Officer's July 2025 guide points out: "AI models do not need an ATO [authority to operate], but the actual system infrastructure layer does," and "adding models to an already approved system will typically not require a new system authorization." The same guide clarifies that it covers cybersecurity only and excludes "AI system performance expectations." The accreditation covers the hosting environment.

Military AI users number in the millions, yet the department cut its independent operational test organization's staff in half. The Government Accountability Office found in April that "well-defined, universal AI tests do not exist yet," and in June that this cut "increases the risk of weapon systems being delivered to the warfighters with undocumented shortfalls." In a January 12 speech, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth named test and evaluation and authority to operate among the barriers to be "treated as operational risks." Three senators called for an inspector general investigation into the intelligence report based on faulty AI answers.

The Models Will Keep Surprising Their Makers

Testing the system is better than testing the model because AI vendors cannot predict what their own models will do. OpenAI reported that models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation bypassed isolation controls and compromised parts of its research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems in July 2026. OpenAI described how agents used a shared message board to exchange exploits. The incident illustrates how a model can behave in ways its developers did not anticipate.

The frontier labs' safety remedies (red lines, better alignment, more monitoring by more models) are all model-level. The department’s strategy calls for the ability to deploy new models within thirty days of release. It should also spell out how those models will be tested independently in military applications. Anthropic proposed embedding outside evaluators, arguing that a second opinion "free of commercial incentives" beats any self-report. The department should apply independent verification to models used in the military, especially any that are used in or inform the killweb.

What a System Test Looks Like, and Who Runs It

The department has made AI available to millions of users. Its public GenAI.mil announcements give little detail about how it tests system performance. A weapon system has to pass an independent operational test before it is fielded. An analyst's finished intelligence product has to meet assurance standards in Intelligence Community Directive 203: document how good the sources are, and keep what is known apart from what is assumed. The department should apply a comparable retesting requirement when it swaps a model in an AI system.

AI systems should be tested the way any other system is: define what right looks like, run a test to verify it behaves as expected, and document the evidence for future reviews. The returned verdict should pass or fail against a documented test metric, while demonstrating the strength of evidence the verdict rests on. A pass on thin evidence should never be mistaken for a pass on all related questions, and a test with no evidence to rule on should say so rather than pass by default. This test survives a model swap because the specification lives outside the model. The specification says what a correct output looks like for this system.

Swap Gemini for ChatGPT for Grok and the specification does not change, so the same specification is run again against the new model, and the comparison shows whether the swap moved the system's behavior, and by how much. The objection that you cannot test a system whose core component changes every month gets it backward. The component is the thing you cannot certify, because it will be different next month. The specification is the thing that stays put, and running it again after every change is the only test that still means anything once the swap has happened.

A test for an intelligence system could check whether cited evidence actually supports a claim about a ship’s cargo. That would help test for the kind of error CNN described.

Some have argued that military units using AI should handle testing themselves, with a single authorized operator who logs prompts, keeps a small test set, tunes prompts until the model’s answers look right, and rolls back a model that is inaccurate or drifting. That is a poor force-wide answer for four reasons: (1) it makes one person in each unit a single point of failure, applied differently across the force, which complicates multi-theater operations; (2) the judgment behind those prompts leaves with every operator's change of station, and the prompts left behind were tuned for a model that’s constantly changing; (3) units lack the authority to roll back a model in a system shared across organizations; and (4) a prompt tuned for one AI model fails on the next, while the department runs several vendors' models concurrently.

Vendor benchmarks alone cannot establish whether an AI system meets a military mission’s requirements. For weapons, operational testing is independent of the program office by law, because a program office and its vendor have every incentive to report that performance meets the requirement. A system test for AI needs the same independence: a tester that owns the specification, runs it on every model change, and reports to the authorizing official. That tester can be the Director of Operational Test and Evaluation, a service operational test agency, a federally funded research and development center, a university-affiliated research center, a contracted third party, or a combination thereof. It has to answer to the government and must have no stake in the model under test. The tools for writing and running a specification are a secondary question. Several already exist, and the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute has released one as open source.

Critics may argue that thirty days is too short to verify a model. That assumes every model swap triggers a scheduled test event, with testers, test windows, and a written report. A specification-based test needs none of that. When a model changes, so does every system that runs on it, such as a custom agent on GenAI.mil or an intelligence system built on the same model. No test workforce, let alone one just cut in half, could review thousands of systems every month. Running a specification-based test doesn't depend on that workforce’s daily capacity, because the specification is programmed once and reruns at machine speed. The systems with the new model undergo the programmed tests, the testing software scores the answers, and the results are delivered to accreditors. Systems that fail stay on the currently approved model while the vendor fixes the model release that failed. The test specification is updated on its own schedule, as the mission changes or test results reveal gaps, and never to fit a particular model.

Write It Down, Fund It, and Own It

Program offices that want AI safety run into the same challenges as most programs: no documented requirement and insufficient authorized and appropriated funding. First, the requirement: the acceleration strategy tells vendors to deliver the newest model, fast, and is silent on verifying outputs by a tester. It should also require that the system be tested against the command's written specification by a government or independent tester, with a record. It is imperative this testing happens before a model is fielded for any use that produces finished intelligence or feeds targeting, and after every model change. That language can go into the next GenAI.mil model release tomorrow, rather than wait for the standards Congress has ordered by June 2027. Second, the money: the department should identify funding for the testing it requires. The department already knows what a failure costs.

Currently, authorizing officials accredit system infrastructure, not the AI models within, nor the answers they produce. The department should make the AI's performance part of what is authorized, similar to how a weapon must meet accuracy thresholds. The definition of a correct answer, the test evidence, and the record should travel with the authorization package, and a model swap that fails against them should be reworked before it is fielded. This approach mirrors what the autonomy directive already requires for weapons. Extending it to the intelligence tools that inform what those weapons do is the same requirement, applied one step earlier.

Specifications, Checks, and a Record

We are not arguing the department should slow down AI implementation. All military users should have the power of AI. What the department should prevent is a wrong answer that tears a hole in the killweb.

The senators called for the inspectors general to investigate. Any investigation comes down to three questions: what were the specifications, who checked the systems met these specifications, and where is the record. Right now, the department can answer the first with a stack of directives and the other two with a shrug. Corrective action is straightforward and ready to implement immediately. The department can update the policy to require that AI models be tested for accuracy, specifying that contracts be updated to reflect this requirement, then apply funding to address this pressing operational need. Improving AI safety will directly drive operational outcomes and protect the department and its people from being misled by AI hallucinations.

item.title: The midterms were a referendum on Trump—and Biden—foreign policy
item.description:
There is no debate as to why Donald Trump and the Republican Party suffered a historic and humiliating defeat at the polls on Tuesday: it all comes down to the Iran war and the cost-of-living crisis it has brought about.

But lost in the conversation is that this was not just a rejection of the Iran war. It was also a repudiation of the broader foreign policy that repeatedly gets the U.S. into wars — or into supporting the wars and war crimes of U.S. partners. In many contests on Tuesday, the U.S.-Israel relationship was on the ballot too, and it was rejected by Republicans and Democrats alike in favor of recentering priorities back to national interests, including ending the flow of military aid to Israel.

Trump famously ran on a promise to end forever wars and not to start new ones. But he ended up listening to the Israeli Prime Minister and started a major war with Iran, even though a diplomatic deal was on the table that was objectively stronger than President Barack Obama’s deal. Trump could have declared victory, but instead he listened to the Israeli government and chose to declare war. Now he is paying for it by losing his majority in Congress.

But it’s not just this election. Since George W. Bush, the American public has voted for presidents — Obama, then Trump and Biden — who have promised less foreign adventurism and more military restraint. Now, with a rejection of the Gaza policy in 2024 and now Iran in 2026, wars are becoming a major, even crucial factor in their voting, according to exit polling.

President Joe Biden repeatedly touted the centrality of human rights in his foreign policy. "That's why, from day one of my administration, I've taken concrete steps to put human rights back at the center of our foreign policy," he said in a speech in October 2021. But when push came to shove, Biden deferred to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and ended up funding and enabling a genocide in Gaza.

A year later, voters punished the Democrats at the polls and paved the way for Trump’s return to the White House.

A YouGov–IMEU Policy Project poll in January 2025 found that, of the 2020 Biden voters who chose not to vote in 2024, a plurality stayed home because of the Democrats’ Gaza policy. Axios reported that the Democrats' own internal election autopsy reportedly concluded Gaza cost them the elections.

So when voters in Texas elect a candidate who proudly rejects money from the America Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and says that “seeing what's happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being,” and when voters in Michigan cheer when their Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed accuses Israel of genocide and apartheid in his victory speech, it is not just a rejection of Trump’s war; it is also a rejection of the foreign policy of Joe Biden, Antony Blinken, and Jake Sullivan.

Both Trump and Biden, in various ways and to various degrees, pursued a hegemonic foreign policy that continued rather than broke with decades of militarism and deference to Israel. And both Trump and Biden’s voters have now rejected this policy paradigm, revalidating the basis for a transpartisan — or postpartisan — push for a new foreign-policy framework centered on responsible statecraft that seeks strength through peace and prosperity through coexistence.

Opportunities for collaboration between Republicans and Democrats responsive to these overwhelming sentiments of the American people will be plentiful in the next two years.

But the first test will be on December 11, when the current continuing resolution for federal government funding expires. Congress has an obligation now to insist on no new money for the Iran War if and when they pass another stopgap to avoid a shutdown.

item.title: Ukraine is running out of time
item.description:
After over four-and-a-half years of entrenched warfare, reports of U.S.-backed peace talks to end Russia's war on Ukraine are back in the news. After Finland and Norway held Europe’s first direct talks with President Vladimir Putin in a year, more trilateral talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are planned for later this month.

While we’ve heard tales of imminent peace time and again, here's hoping American emissaries and their counterparts can finally bring an end to the fighting.That’s because, despite considerable efforts by the U.S. and Europe to help Ukraine win this war, there is no victory in sight. While Ukrainians arguably thwarted Russian advances in its very first weeks, its backers have failed to help Ukraine consolidate its battlefield victories at the negotiating table.

As a result, Russia’s invasion has slowly wrecked Ukraine: the war is Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II and Russia has seized approximately a fifth of Ukraine’s territory. After years of needless death and destruction, what will it take to actually forge an agreement to finally end this war?

For the latest episode of Always at War, we spoke to Anatol Lieven, journalist, author, professor, and now Director of the Eurasia Program at the Quincy Institute to discuss his career, how he became an expert on the region, and what he thinks peace can look like there.

Lieven’s diagnosis of Ukraine’s current situation is grim. He estimates that the war has killed some 200,000-250,000 Ukrainians, that millions have fled the country and are unlikely to return, and explains that the birthrate has completely collapsed. As he puts it, “the population may be half what it was in 1990.”

But what’s most shocking about the dire circumstances facing Kyiv is that they were foreseeable, and perhaps even preventable. Lieven himself predicted many of the current crises over decades of analysis, from books including Russia and Ukraine: A Fraternal Rivalry in 1999, to Quincy Institute papers on the dangers of protracted war in 2022.

What was true then is still true today: a compromise peace that secures Kyiv’s sovereignty and empowers Ukrainians to rebuild and return is a victory for Ukraine.

As Lieven has long insisted, pretending this would be anything but a victory is foolhardy: most wars “have ended not with the complete victory of one side, but with some form of messy compromise.”

Yet instead of coming to grips with the realities facing Ukraine, popular headlines continue to push narratives promising imminent victory. One possible explanation for the media’s incessant optimism is that Ukraine’s victory, understandably, feels like a moral imperative in response to Russia’s unjust war. As a result, journalists and world leaders alike are willing to indulge fantasy rather than acknowledge the gruesome truth on the ground. But Ukrainians themselves don’t have the luxury of retreating to fantasy; by a 2:1 margin, they would rather see their government prioritize ending the war as soon as possible instead of pursuing total victory.

The continued refusal by many in Washington to recognize Ukrainians’ appetites for peace, and the realities on the ground informing them, constitute a noble lie to oneself, one’s readers, or one’s constituents. It’s a lie that’s gone too far.

item.title: I know the dangers a wounded Trump presents – this is how the UK should deal with him now | Kim Darroch
item.description:
Power is draining away at home, but the US president will see a chance to make his mark through foreign policy

  • Kim Darroch was Britain’s ambassador to the US between January 2016 and December 2019

Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half the guests had left.

In contrast, I recall speaking to Nancy Pelosi, the queen of the Democrats, at a watch party on 6 November 2018, for the midterms during Trump’s first presidency. I asked her what I should put in my overnight report to London, given that most results wouldn’t be in. She said, with striking confidence, that I should predict that the Democrats would retake the House of Representatives. She was right: the Democrats flipped 41 Republican seats. It gave Pelosi a second term as speaker of the House and gave the world the enjoyable theatre of her sitting directly behind Trump at his State of the Union speeches, rolling her eyes at the bombast.

Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump

item.title: The Guardian view on the midterms and foreign policy: American voters spoke, and now the world waits anxiously | Editorial
item.description:
The Democrats have gained new powers to constrain Donald Trump. But the drubbing that Republicans received could yet prompt him to new excesses

Donald Trump is a president without parallel, but history can still be instructive. Lame duck presidents often focus on foreign policy to escape domestic discontent and establish a legacy in an area where a hostile Congress offers less of an obstacle. Mr Trump, who was stunningly rebuffed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms, might seek satisfaction in construction projects, the 2028 presidential race and his family’s future. Or, amid the humiliation and with Republican critics growing louder, he could distract attention with fresh adventurism – perhaps escalating against Cuba – or more likely a vengeful new offensive against Iran.

Mr Trump won’t put in the legwork or attention to detail demanded by, say, Bill Clinton’s push for lasting peace in the Middle East. But he loves the glitz of state visits, spectacular military action, hobnobbing with strongmen and (unearned) credit for dubious “peace deals”. With a potential three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping mooted for the Apec summit in China this month, Ukraine, Taiwan and others have reason to be nervous.
